Title: Get the Facts: Are there more manufacturing jobs in the US?

Since President Donald Trump announced 'reciprocal' tariffs in April 2024, manufacturing employment in the U.S. has declined, according to an analysis by the Get the Facts Data Team using Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data. Employment stood at approximately 12.2 million when President Joe Biden began his term and increased to about 12.7 million by the end of December 2024. However, by February 2026, the number had dropped by 108,000, with job losses occurring each month since January 2025, though 5,000 jobs were added in the most recent month. Josh Bivens, chief economist at the nonpartisan Economic Policy Institute, attributed the decline to a softening labor market and noted that tariffs are currently doing more harm than good by increasing production costs and triggering retaliatory measures. While job growth stabilized through 2019 under Trump’s first term, it has since declined. More than half of U.S. states saw a drop in manufacturing employment over the past year: Alaska led with a 6% decline (800 jobs lost), followed by Montana (5%) and Oregon (3%). California, Texas, and Ohio have the highest total manufacturing employment, but only Ohio reported growth (8,500 jobs), while California lost 32,600 jobs (2.3% decline). Bivens emphasized that manufacturing remains a critical sector for workers without college degrees, and job losses often result in lower-paying, less secure employment. The article concludes that Trump’s tariff policy lacks a coherent strategy and appears erratic.

Title: US adds 130,000 jobs and unemployment falls after tepid 2025

Summary: 
The U.S. labor market showed signs of stabilization in January 2026, with employers adding 130,000 jobs—the largest gain in over a year—and the unemployment rate unexpectedly falling to 4.3%, according to Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data. This follows a tepid 2025, during which average monthly job gains were just 15,000, down from an initial estimate of 49,000. The January improvement was driven primarily by health care, which added the most jobs since 2020, along with gains in construction, professional and business services, and manufacturing—marking its first monthly employment increase in over a year. Federal government payrolls continued to decline. The report also revealed a 0.4% rise in average hourly earnings and a notable drop in part-time workers due to economic reasons—the largest since June 2022. The labor force participation rate edged up to 62.5%, and the number of people unemployed for 27 weeks or more declined. The BLS made widespread revisions to prior data, including updating its birth-death model, which accounts for net business openings and closures, improving the model’s responsiveness. The January report was delayed due to the partial government shutdown and included benchmark adjustments based on the Quarterly Census of Employment and Wages, which showed job growth in the 12 months through March 2025 was nearly 900,000 lower than initially reported. Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell cited the data as evidence of a steadying labor market, reinforcing the Fed’s decision to keep interest rates unchanged. President Donald Trump praised the report on social media, calling it 'GREAT JOBS NUMBERS, FAR GREATER THAN EXPECTED!' and reiterating calls for lower interest rates. Economists remain cautious, noting the growth is lopsided, with health care dominating, and warning that layoffs remain constrained but still present, as seen in recent announcements by Amazon, UPS, and others. The household survey also showed increased job mobility, with more people leaving their jobs, suggesting confidence in finding new work. The report was originally scheduled for February 6 but was delayed by one month due to the government shutdown. Officials from the Trump administration have also attempted to reset expectations for future reports, citing projected lower population growth and the impact of deportations.

The report noted that the industrial sector has lost jobs every month since March 2024, indicating a prolonged contraction trend. ADP's chief economist, Nela Richardson, stated that job creation slowed in 2025, with private employers adding 398,000 positions compared to 771,000 in 2024. She emphasized a 'continuous and dramatic slowdown in job creation over the past three years,' despite stable wage growth. The U.S. government is scheduled to release official labor market data on Friday, but the release may be delayed due to a temporary government shutdown.
